results.title: Terms for unification
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a type $C$ of constants, a term over $C$ is either a variable $x$, indexed by a natural number $x \in \mathbb{N}$, or a constant $c \in C$, or a binary node built from two terms $l$ and $r$.

results.title: Substitution
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A substitution is a map assigning a term to every variable, that is, a function from the set $\mathbb{N}$ of variables to terms.

results.title: Applying a substitution to a term
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a substitution $\sigma$ and a term $t$, the term $t\sigma$ is obtained from $t$ by replacing every variable $x$ by $\sigma(x)$: a variable $x$ becomes $\sigma(x)$, a constant is unchanged, and a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ becomes the node with subterms $l\sigma$ and $r\sigma$.

results.title: Size of a term
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a term is the number of symbols in it: a variable and a constant have size $1$, and a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ has size equal to the size of $l$ plus the size of $r$ plus $1$.

results.title: Variables of a term
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The variables of a term form a finite set of natural numbers, defined recursively: the variable $x$ has the variable set $\{x\}$, a constant has no variables, and the variables of a node with subterms $l$ and $r$ are those of $l$ together with those of $r$.

results.title: Substitution depends only on the variables of the term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If two substitutions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ agree on every variable occurring in a term $u$, then applying $\sigma$ to $u$ gives the same term as applying $\tau$ to $u$.

results.title: Variables of a substituted term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a substitution and $t$ a term. Every variable of the term obtained by applying $s$ to $t$ is a variable of $s(y)$ for some variable $y$ of $t$.

results.title: Variables of a substituted variable occur in the substituted term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every substitution $s$, term $t$ and variable $y$ occurring in $t$, every variable of the term $s(y)$ occurs in the term obtained from $t$ by applying $s$.

results.title: Occurs check: size bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable and $t$ a term in which $x$ occurs, with $t$ not the variable $x$ itself. Then for every substitution $\sigma$, the term $\sigma(x)$ has strictly smaller size than $t\sigma$, the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$.

results.title: Substituting for a variable that does not occur in the substituted term
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable and $t$ a term in which $x$ does not occur. For every term $u$, every variable of the term obtained from $u$ by replacing each occurrence of $x$ with $t$ is a variable of $u$ or of $t$, and is different from $x$.

results.title: Composition of substitutions on first-order terms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For substitutions $s$ and $t$, the composite $s \gg t$ (first $s$, then $t$) sends each variable $x$ to the term obtained from $s(x)$ by applying $t$ to every variable of $s(x)$.

results.title: Single-variable substitution on first-order terms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a variable $x$ and a term $t$, the substitution $[x \mapsto t]$ sends $x$ to $t$ and every other variable $y$ to the term $y$.

results.title: Absorbing a single-variable substitution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable, $t$ a term, and $[x \mapsto t]$ the substitution replacing $x$ by $t$ and fixing every other variable. If a substitution $\sigma$ satisfies $\sigma(x) = t\sigma$, where $t\sigma$ is the result of applying $\sigma$ to $t$, then the composite substitution that applies $[x \mapsto t]$ first and $\sigma$ second equals $\sigma$.

results.title: A term is fixed by substituting it for a variable it avoids
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the variable $x$ does not occur in the term $t$, then applying to $t$ the substitution $[x \mapsto t]$, which replaces $x$ by $t$ and fixes every other variable, leaves $t$ unchanged.

results.title: Lists of equations
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A list of equations over constants $C$ is a finite list of pairs $(t, u)$ of terms over $C$, each pair standing for the equation $t = u$.

results.title: Unifier of a list of equations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A substitution $s$ unifies a list $E$ of equations between terms when, for every equation $(t, u)$ in $E$, applying $s$ to $t$ and applying $s$ to $u$ give the same term.

results.title: Most general unifier
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A substitution $s$ is a most general unifier of a list of equations $E$ when $s$ unifies $E$ and every unifier $s'$ of $E$ factors through $s$, that is, $s' = s \gg r$ for some substitution $r$, where $s \gg r$ applies first $s$ and then $r$.

results.title: Applying a substitution to a list of equations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a substitution $\sigma$ and a list $E$ of equations between terms, the result is the list obtained by replacing each equation $u = v$ of $E$, in order, by $u\sigma = v\sigma$, where $u\sigma$ is the result of applying $\sigma$ to $u$.

results.title: Variables of a list of equations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The variables of a list of equations form the finite set of all variables that occur on either side of any of its equations.

results.title: Total size of a list of equations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The total size of a list of equations is the sum, over all its equations, of the sizes of the two sides, where the size of a term is its number of variable, constant and node symbols.

results.title: Eliminating a solved variable lowers the number of variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a variable, $t$ a term in which $x$ does not occur, and $E$ a list of equations. Applying the substitution that replaces $x$ by $t$ (and fixes every other variable) to both sides of every equation of $E$ gives a list of equations with strictly fewer distinct variables than the list obtained by putting the equation $x = t$ in front of $E$.

results.title: Specification of a unification result
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a list of equations between terms and $r$ either a substitution or failure. The specification holds for $E$ and $r$ when, if $r$ is a substitution $s$, then $s$ unifies $E$ and every substitution $s'$ that unifies $E$ equals the composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s'$; and, if $r$ is failure, then no substitution unifies $E$.

results.title: Failure is correct when the first equation has no unifier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a list of equations between terms and let $u = v$ be a further equation, where $u\sigma$ denotes the result of applying a substitution $\sigma$ to $u$. If $u\sigma \ne v\sigma$ for every substitution $\sigma$, then returning no substitution meets the unification specification for the list obtained by putting $u = v$ in front of $E$: no substitution unifies that list.

results.title: Soundness of unification
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $E$ of equations between terms, if the Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then $s$ unifies $E$: applying $s$ to the two sides of any equation of $E$ gives the same term.

results.title: Most generality of unification
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $E$ of equations between terms, if the Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then every substitution $s'$ that unifies $E$ equals the composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s'$.

results.title: Unification returns a most general unifier
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the Martelli-Montanari unification algorithm, run on a list of equations $E$, returns a substitution $s$, then $s$ is a most general unifier of $E$.

results.title: Unification returns an idempotent substitution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $E$ of equations between terms, if the Martelli–Montanari algorithm returns a substitution $s$ on $E$, then $s$ is idempotent: the composite substitution that applies first $s$ and then $s$ equals $s$.

results.title: Completeness of unification
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $E$ of equations between terms, the Martelli–Montanari algorithm fails on $E$ if and only if no substitution unifies $E$.

results.title: Unification introduces no new variables
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a list of equations between terms. If the unification algorithm succeeds on $E$ and returns the substitution $s$, then for every variable $x$, each variable of the term $s(x)$ is either $x$ itself or a variable occurring in some equation of $E$.

results.title: Divided-power ideal
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An ideal $I$ of a commutative ring $A$ is a *divided-power ideal* when for every $a \in I$ and every integer $k \ge 1$ there is $c \in I$ with $a^k = k! \, c$, that is, $a^k \in k! \, I$. For a prime $p$, in a torsion-free $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebra this says $a^k / k! \in I$.

results.title: The zero ideal is a divided-power ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: In every commutative ring, the zero ideal is a divided-power ideal.

results.title: Ideals with divided powers are divided-power ideals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $I$ be an ideal of a commutative ring $A$. If $I$ carries a divided-power structure $(\gamma_k)_{k \ge 0}$ in the usual sense, then $I$ is a divided-power ideal: for every $a \in I$ and every $k \ge 1$ there is $c \in I$ with $a^k = k!\, c$.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every monic polynomial $P$ over a commutative ring, $e_0(P) = 1$.

results.title: Elementary symmetric functions vanish above the degree

results.title: A prime-exponent criterion for powers in an ideal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime, $v_p$ the $p$-adic valuation, and $\mathfrak{b}$ an ideal of a commutative ring $B$. The following are equivalent: for every $n \ge 1$ and every $a \in \mathfrak{b}$ there is $c \in \mathfrak{b}$ with $a^n = p^{v_p(n!)} c$; and for every $a \in \mathfrak{b}$ there is $c \in \mathfrak{b}$ with $a^p = p c$.

results.title: The $p$-th power criterion for divided-power ideals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $A$ be a commutative ring in which every natural number not divisible by $p$ is a unit (a $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebra). An ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ of $A$ is a divided-power ideal if and only if for every $a \in \mathfrak{a}$ there is $c \in \mathfrak{a}$ with $a^p = p\,c$, that is, $a^p \in p\mathfrak{a}$.

results.title: Divided-power ideals generated by a set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and $A$ a commutative ring in which every natural number not divisible by $p$ is a unit (a $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-algebra). For a subset $S \subseteq A$, the ideal $\mathfrak{a}$ generated by $S$ is a divided-power ideal if and only if for every $a \in S$ there is $c \in \mathfrak{a}$ with $a^p = pc$, that is, $a^p \in p\mathfrak{a}$.

results.title: Product of a divided-power ideal with an ideal

results.title: Powers of the maximal ideal of a DVR that are divided-power ideals

results.title: When the maximal ideal of a DVR is a divided-power ideal

results.title: Primitive polynomials via primitive roots of unity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F$ be a finite field with $q$ elements, let $f \in F[X]$, and let $n$ be the degree of $f$ (with $n = 0$ if $f = 0$). results.title: The weak order on the symmetric group is Sperner
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$ and every antichain $A$ of the weak order on the symmetric group $S_n$ of permutations of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$ (where $\sigma \le \tau$ when the inversion set of $\sigma$ is contained in that of $\tau$), there is a $k$ such that $A$ has at most as many elements as there are permutations with exactly $k$ inversions.

results.title: Balanced graph
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and $D$ a real number. The graph $G$ is $D$-balanced if its maximum degree $\Delta(G)$ is at most $D$ times its minimum degree $\delta(G)$, that is, $\Delta(G) \le D \cdot \delta(G)$.

results.title: Nondeterministic time hierarchy
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Source: S. A. Cook, "A hierarchy for nondeterministic time complexity", Journal of Computer and System Sciences 7 (1973), 343-353; S. Zak, "A Turing machine time hierarchy", Theoretical Computer Science 26 (1983), 327-333.

results.title: Interval
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An interval is a pair of integers, its low endpoint and its high endpoint, read as the closed interval from the low to the high endpoint. The structure itself imposes no order on the endpoints; the public update operations accept an interval only when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.

results.title: Valid interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A closed interval with integer endpoints $a$ (low) and $b$ (high) is valid when its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint, $a \le b$.

results.title: Boolean interval validity test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an interval $[a, b]$ with integer endpoints, the Boolean validity test returns true exactly when $a \le b$.

results.title: Overlapping closed intervals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ overlaps an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$ when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; in particular, intervals that share only an endpoint overlap.

results.title: Overlap test for closed intervals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns true exactly when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; it compares $a$ with $d$ first and returns false without the second comparison when $a > d$.

results.title: Overlap test with comparison count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an interval $I$ with low endpoint $a$ and high endpoint $b$ and an interval $J$ with low endpoint $c$ and high endpoint $d$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ returns the pair (false, $1$) when $a > d$, the pair (false, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c > b$, and the pair (true, $2$) when $a \le d$ and $c \le b$; the number is the count of endpoint comparisons evaluated.

results.title: The instrumented overlap test returns the plain result
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the Boolean component of the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ equals the overlap test of $I$ against $J$.

results.title: Comparison count of the overlap test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For intervals $I$ and $J$, the instrumented overlap test of $I$ against $J$ reports $2$ endpoint comparisons when the low endpoint of $I$ is at most the high endpoint of $J$, and $1$ comparison otherwise.

results.title: Interval tree entry
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An entry of the interval tree consists of an identifier, which is a natural number, and an interval with integer low and high endpoints.

results.title: Search key of an interval entry
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The key of an entry is the pair $(\ell, i) \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$, where $\ell$ is the low endpoint of the entry's interval and $i$ is the entry's identifier.

results.title: Lexicographic comparison of keys
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For keys $(a, i)$ and $(b, j)$ in $\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ (a low endpoint and an occurrence identifier), the comparison returns less-than if $a < b$, or if $a = b$ and $i < j$; greater-than if $a > b$, or if $a = b$ and $i > j$; and equal if $a = b$ and $i = j$.

results.title: Operation cost counters for interval trees
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A cost record for the interval tree consists of seven natural-number counters, each defaulting to $0$: node visits, key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations, and identifier-index operations.

results.title: Interval tree
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: An interval tree is either empty or a node consisting of a left subtree, an entry, a right subtree and three cached fields: a height and a size (natural numbers) and a maximum high endpoint (an integer). The type imposes no balance or consistency condition on these fields; it is the carrier on which the AVL interval-tree operations act.

results.title: Cached maximum of an interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The cached maximum of an interval tree is no value when the tree is empty, and when the tree is a node it is the integer stored in the node's cached maximum-high-endpoint field.

results.title: Maximum with an optional value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an integer $a$ and an optional integer $v$, the value is $a$ when $v$ is absent and $\max(a, v)$ when $v$ is present. It combines a value with an optional subtree maximum without using a sentinel value.

results.title: Maximum high endpoint at a node
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For subtrees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, the node maximum is the largest of the high endpoint of the interval of $e$, the cached maximum high endpoint stored at the root of $L$, and the one stored at the root of $R$, where an empty subtree stores no cached maximum and contributes nothing.

results.title: Node construction with repaired metadata
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an interval tree $T$ write $h(T)$ and $|T|$ for its cached height and size, both $0$ for the empty tree. Given interval trees $L$ and $R$ and an entry $e$, this builds the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ whose cached height is $\max(h(L), h(R)) + 1$, whose cached size is $|L| + |R| + 1$, and whose cached maximum high endpoint is the largest of the high endpoint of $e$ and the cached…

results.title: Cache invariant of an interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An interval tree satisfies the cache invariant when every cached field is exact, recursively. The empty tree satisfies it. A node with stored height $h$, stored size $s$, stored maximum $m$, left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$ satisfies it when $L$ and $R$ satisfy it, $m$ is at least the high endpoint of every entry of $L$, of $e$ and of every entry of $R$, $m$ equals the high endpoint of one of these…

results.title: Low-endpoint ordered interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty tree is low-endpoint ordered, and a node is low-endpoint ordered when both of its subtrees are low-endpoint ordered, every interval in the left subtree has low endpoint at most the low endpoint of the node's interval, and the node's low endpoint is at most the low endpoint of every interval in the right subtree.

results.title: Validity invariant of an interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree satisfies the validity invariant when every interval stored in it is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint. Recursively, the empty tree satisfies it, and a node satisfies it when its left subtree does, the interval of its entry is valid, and its right subtree does.

results.title: Right rotation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$ to $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.

results.title: Left rotation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, c\rangle$, where both nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.

results.title: Left-right double rotation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The left-right rotation sends $\langle\langle a, x, \langle b, y, c\rangle\rangle, z, d\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.

results.title: Right-left double rotation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $\langle L, x, R\rangle$ for a node with left subtree $L$, entry $x$ and right subtree $R$. The right-left rotation sends $\langle a, x, \langle\langle b, y, c\rangle, z, d\rangle\rangle$ to $\langle\langle a, x, b\rangle, y, \langle c, z, d\rangle\rangle$, where all three nodes of the result get freshly recomputed height, size and maximum high endpoint. Every tree not of this shape is returned unchanged.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Removing the leftmost entry of an interval tree $T$ returns nothing when $T$ is empty. results.title: Instrumented search in the empty tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every query interval $q$, the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the empty interval tree returns no entry, and its cost record counts one node visit and zero for every other counter (key comparisons, endpoint comparisons, cached-maximum reads, cache writes, rotations and index operations).

results.title: Interval-tree overlap search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The overlap search of a query interval $q$ in an interval tree $T$ returns the optional entry produced by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in $T$, discarding its cost record.

results.title: Linear-scan overlap search
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree $T$ and a query interval $q$, the oracle search returns the first entry, in the in-order list of entries of $T$, whose interval overlaps $q$ as closed intervals, and returns nothing when no entry's interval overlaps $q$.

results.title: Key between optional bounds
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an optional lower bound, an optional upper bound and a key $k$ (a pair of an integer and a natural number), this test returns true exactly when the lower bound is absent or strictly below $k$, and the upper bound is absent or strictly above $k$. Keys are compared lexicographically: first by the integer, then by the natural number.

results.title: Ordered-and-valid check for interval trees
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Boolean AVL balance check for interval trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The balance check returns true on the empty tree. On a node whose left and right subtrees have stored heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ (the empty tree has height $0$), it returns true exactly when the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and the check returns true on both subtrees.

results.title: AVL balance of an interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An interval tree is AVL balanced with exact stored heights when it is empty, or when it is a node such that, writing $h_L$ and $h_R$ for the stored heights of its left and right subtrees (the empty tree has height $0$), the node's stored height equals $\max(h_L, h_R) + 1$, $h_L \le h_R + 1$, $h_R \le h_L + 1$, and both subtrees are again AVL balanced with exact stored heights.

results.title: Key-ordered interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The empty tree is key-ordered, and a node is key-ordered when both of its subtrees are key-ordered, the key of every entry in the left subtree is strictly less than the key of the node's entry, and the key of the node's entry is strictly less than the key of every entry in the right subtree. Keys are compared lexicographically: low endpoint first, then identifier.

results.caption: Theorem

If the executable ordering check of $t$ with lower bound $\ell$ and upper bound $u$ succeeds, then $t$ is low-endpoint ordered, and every entry $e$ stored in $t$ satisfies $\ell < \operatorname{key}(e)$ when $\ell$ is present and $\operatorname{key}(e) < u$ when $u$ is present, where $<$ is the lexicographic order…

results.title: The ordering check implies interval validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree and let $\ell$ and $u$ be optional lower and upper key bounds. If the executable check of $T$ with bounds $\ell$ and $u$, which tests that every key lies strictly between its bounds and that every stored interval passes the Boolean validity test, returns true, then every interval stored in $T$ is valid, that is, its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint.

results.title: Removing the minimum preserves the other entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If removing the leftmost entry of a tree $T$ returns an entry $m$, a tree $T'$ and a cost, then the list consisting of $m$ followed by the in-order entries of $T'$ is a permutation of the in-order entries of $T$.

results.title: Entries after keyed insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a tree whose entries are strictly ordered by key, and let $x$ be an entry. The in-order list of entries of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ by key is a permutation of the list consisting of $x$ followed by those entries of $t$ whose key differs from the key of $x$.

results.title: Strictly key-ordered trees have distinct keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a tree is strictly ordered by key, then the keys of its stored entries are pairwise distinct.

results.title: Insertion into an interval tree preserves key ordering

results.title: Removing the minimum from an interval tree preserves key ordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree. If the cost-instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds, returning that entry, a remaining tree $t'$ and a cost, then $t'$ is key-ordered.

results.title: Deletion from an interval tree preserves key ordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a key-ordered interval tree and let $k \in \mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{N}$ be a key. Then the tree returned by the cost-instrumented keyed deletion of $k$ from $t$ (the reported cost is discarded) is again key-ordered.

results.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be interval trees that are AVL balanced with exact stored heights, with heights $h_L$ and $h_R$ satisfying $h_L \le h_R + 2$ and $h_R \le h_L + 2$, and let $e$ be an entry. Let $B$ be the tree obtained by rebalancing the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored). Then $B$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, the height…

results.title: Keyed insertion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $e$ be an entry. The tree $T'$ returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (which replaces an entry with the same key, if there is one; we take the tree component of the result and ignore the cost) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one more.

results.title: Removing the minimum preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights. If removing the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds and returns an entry $m$, a remaining tree $R$ and a cost $c$, then $R$ is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $R$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.

results.title: Keyed deletion preserves AVL balance in an interval tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree that is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree $T'$ returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) is again AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and the height of $T'$ is either the height of $T$ or one less.

results.title: Node construction preserves interval validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $L$ and $R$ are interval trees satisfying the validity invariant and $e$ is an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, then the node with left subtree $L$, entry $e$ and right subtree $R$, built by the node constructor that recomputes the cached fields, satisfies the validity invariant.

results.title: Stored intervals of a valid tree are valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $T$ satisfies the validity invariant, then every entry stored in $T$ has an interval $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.

results.title: Keyed insertion preserves interval validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$, and let $e$ be an entry whose interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then the tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.

results.title: Removing the minimum preserves interval validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If the instrumented removal of the leftmost entry of $T$ succeeds, returning that entry $m$, the remaining tree $T'$ and a cost record $c$, then every interval stored in $T'$ is valid.

results.title: Keyed erasure preserves interval validity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree in which every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfies $a \le b$. Then for every key $(\ell, i)$ with $\ell$ an integer and $i$ a natural number, the tree returned by keyed erasure of $(\ell, i)$ from $T$ also has every stored interval $[a, b]$ satisfying $a \le b$.

results.title: Indexed interval tree
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: An indexed interval tree consists of a root interval tree together with an identifier index: a finite map, implemented as a balanced search tree, from natural-number identifiers to integer low endpoints.

results.title: Insertion by identifier with cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree and let $e$ be an entry with identifier $i$ and interval $[a, b]$. Inserting $e$ into $T$ first tests $a \le b$. If $a > b$, it returns no tree, at a cost of one endpoint comparison. Otherwise, if the identifier index of $T$ maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the root tree of $T$ by keyed erasure; if $i$ is not in the index, the root…

results.title: Erasure by identifier with cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: To erase identifier $i$ from an indexed interval tree, look $i$ up in the identifier index. If it is absent, the tree is returned unchanged at a cost of one index operation. If the index maps $i$ to a low endpoint $\ell$, the entry with key $(\ell, i)$ is erased from the underlying interval tree, $i$ is removed from the index, and the cost is the cost of the keyed erasure plus two index operations.

results.title: Forward identifier-index check
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the forward index check returns true exactly when the identifier index maps the identifier of every stored entry to the low endpoint of that entry's interval.

results.title: Backward identifier-index check
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the backward index check returns true exactly when, for every identifier $i$ that the identifier index maps to a low endpoint $\ell$, some stored entry has identifier $i$ and an interval with low endpoint $\ell$.

results.title: Representation check for the indexed interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an indexed interval tree, the check returns true exactly when all of the following hold: at every node the cached height and size agree with the values recomputed from its children's cached heights and sizes, and the cached maximum high endpoint equals the largest of the node's own high endpoint and its children's cached maxima; the tree is AVL-balanced (sibling heights differ by at most one) with exact stored…

results.title: Representation invariant of an indexed interval tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An indexed interval tree $T$ satisfies the representation invariant when its root tree has exact cached metadata (heights, sizes, and attained maximum high endpoints), is strictly ordered by the composite key (low endpoint, then identifier), is AVL balanced with exact stored heights, and stores only valid intervals; the identifiers of the stored entries are pairwise distinct; the identifier index maps the…

results.title: The interval-tree smart constructor preserves the cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If interval trees $L$ and $R$ satisfy the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), then for every entry $e$ the node that the smart constructor builds from $L$, $e$ and $R$ also satisfies the cache invariant.

results.title: The executable cache check implies the cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the executable cache check returns true on an interval tree $t$, then $t$ satisfies the cache invariant.

results.title: Right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty left subtree.

results.title: Left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged when $t$ is empty or has an empty right subtree.

results.title: Left-right rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the left-right double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty left subtree whose right subtree is nonempty.

results.title: Right-left rotation preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then so does the right-left double rotation of $t$, which leaves $t$ unchanged unless $t$ has a nonempty right subtree whose left subtree is nonempty.

results.title: Rebalancing preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If an interval tree $t$ satisfies the cache invariant, then the tree returned by the rebalancing step at the root of $t$ also satisfies the cache invariant.

results.title: Keyed insertion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $e$ be an entry. The tree returned by keyed insertion of $e$ into $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes the case where an entry with the same key is replaced.

results.title: Removing the minimum preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be an interval tree that satisfies the cache invariant. If removing the leftmost entry of $t$ succeeds and returns an entry, a tree $t'$ and an operation cost, then $t'$ satisfies the cache invariant.

results.title: Keyed deletion preserves the interval-tree cache invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an interval tree satisfying the cache invariant (every cached maximum high endpoint, height and size is exact), and let $k$ be a key (a pair of an integer low endpoint and a natural-number identifier). The tree returned by keyed deletion of $k$ from $T$ (the tree component of the result; the cost is ignored) also satisfies the cache invariant. This includes keys that do not occur in $T$.

results.title: Soundness of the invariant checker
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If the executable checker returns true on an indexed interval tree $T$, then $T$ satisfies the representation invariant.

results.title: Soundness of indexed interval-tree search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The search of an indexed interval tree $T$ for a query interval $q = [c, d]$ returns nothing when $c > d$, and otherwise returns the entry, if any, found by the instrumented overlap search of $q$ in the root tree of $T$. For every indexed interval tree $T$, every query interval $q$ and every entry $e$, if this search returns $e$, then $e$ is one of the entries stored in the root tree of $T$ and the interval of $e$…

results.title: Completeness of indexed interval search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying its representation invariant, and let $Q$ be a valid query interval (low endpoint at most high endpoint). If some entry stored in $T$ has an interval that overlaps $Q$ (each interval's low endpoint is at most the other's high endpoint), then searching $T$ for $Q$ returns some entry.

results.title: Correctness of insertion into an indexed interval tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $x$ be an entry whose interval is valid (its low endpoint is at most its high endpoint). If inserting $x$ into $T$ succeeds with result $T'$, then $T'$ satisfies the representation invariant, $x$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$, and an entry $e$ is stored in the root tree of $T'$ if and only if either $e = x$, or $e$ is stored…

results.title: Correctness of erasure from the indexed interval tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $T$ be an indexed interval tree satisfying the representation invariant, and let $i$ be a natural number. Then the tree obtained by erasing identifier $i$ from $T$ again satisfies the invariant, and an entry is stored in it if and only if it is stored in $T$ and its identifier differs from $i$.

results.title: Objective of nonnegative matrix factorization
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The NMF objective: the squared Frobenius distance `‖X - W H‖_F² = ∑ i j, (X i j - (W H) i j)²` between the data `X` and the product `W * H`.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the NMF objective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The objective is nonnegative.

results.title: The NMF objective is invariant under transposition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Transposing exchanges the roles of `W` and `H`: `‖Xᵀ - Hᵀ Wᵀ‖² = ‖X - W H‖²`.

results.title: Existence of a minimizer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real matrix `X` and every finite inner index type `k`, the objective attains its infimum over pairs `W, H ≥ 0` (entrywise).

results.title: Lee–Seung multiplicative update of H
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Lee–Seung multiplicative update of `H` (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1): `H a j ← H a j * (Wᵀ X) a j / (Wᵀ W H) a j`. An entry with a zero denominator becomes `0` (Lean's `x / 0 = 0`).

results.title: Lee–Seung multiplicative update of W
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Lee–Seung multiplicative update of `W` (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1): `W i a ← W i a * (X Hᵀ) i a / (W H Hᵀ) i a`. An entry with a zero denominator becomes `0`.

results.title: One sweep of the Lee–Seung algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: One sweep of the Lee–Seung algorithm: update `H`, then update `W` using the new `H`.

results.title: The W update is the H update of the transposed problem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The `W` update is the `H` update of the transposed problem.

results.title: The Lee–Seung H update preserves nonnegativity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The `H` update keeps `H` nonnegative when `X`, `W`, `H` are nonnegative.

results.title: The Lee–Seung W update preserves nonnegativity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The `W` update keeps `W` nonnegative when `X`, `W`, `H` are nonnegative.

results.title: Lee–Seung, `H` step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Lee–Seung, `H` step (Lee and Seung 2001, Theorem 1): for `W, H ≥ 0`, the multiplicative update of `H` does not increase `‖X - W H‖_F²`. The proof is the auxiliary-function argument: the quadratic term of the exact expansion is bounded by Lee and Seung's diagonal majorant (here through a weighted Cauchy–Schwarz inequality), and the update minimizes the majorant. `X` may have any sign.

results.title: Lee–Seung, `W` step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `W, H ≥ 0`, the multiplicative update of `W` does not increase `‖X - W H‖_F²`.

results.title: A Lee–Seung sweep preserves nonnegativity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One sweep keeps both factors nonnegative when `X ≥ 0`.

results.title: One Lee–Seung sweep does not increase the objective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: One Lee–Seung sweep does not increase the objective, for `X, W, H ≥ 0`.

results.title: The objective is non-increasing along the Lee–Seung iterates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The objective is non-increasing along the Lee–Seung iterates started from `W, H ≥ 0`, for `X ≥ 0`.

results.title: Gradient of the NMF objective with respect to H
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The gradient of the objective with respect to `H`: `2 (Wᵀ W H - Wᵀ X)`.

results.title: Gradient of the NMF objective with respect to W
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The gradient of the objective with respect to `W`: `2 (W H Hᵀ - X Hᵀ)`.

results.title: Partial derivative of the NMF objective in an entry of H
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `gradH X W H a j` is the partial derivative of the objective in the entry `H a j`.

results.title: Partial derivative of the NMF objective in an entry of W
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `gradW X W H i a` is the partial derivative of the objective in the entry `W i a`.

results.title: Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `H` update
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `updateH X W H = H`, then `H a j * gradH X W H a j = 0` for every entry.

results.title: Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `W` update
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Complementary slackness at a fixed point of the `W` update.

results.title: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker point of nonnegative matrix factorization
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions of `min ‖X - W H‖_F²` subject to `W, H ≥ 0`: primal feasibility, dual feasibility (nonnegative gradients) and complementary slackness.

results.title: Positive fixed points are KKT points
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A fixed point of the Lee–Seung sweep with all entries of `W` and `H` positive has both gradients zero, so it satisfies the KKT conditions.

results.title: Separable factor matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: `H` is separable: every factor `a` has a pure column, a column `j` of `H` equal to a positive multiple of the unit vector `e_a`. For `X = W * H` this makes column `j` of `X` a positive multiple of column `a` of `W` (a sample containing only factor `a`). Applied to `Wᵀ` it says that every factor has a pure row of `W` (an "anchor" feature of factor `a` alone).

results.title: A nonnegative matrix with a nonnegative inverse is monomial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If `G * K = 1` with `G` and `K` entrywise nonnegative, then there are a permutation `σ` and positive weights `d` with `G a b = d b` if `a = σ b` and `0` otherwise.

results.title: Essential uniqueness of NMF when both factors are separable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Suppose `X = W * H`, where `W` has a pure row for every factor (`IsSeparable Wᵀ`: for each `a` a row `i` with `W i · = e • e_a`, `e > 0`) and `H` has a pure column for every factor (`IsSeparable H`). Then every factorization `X = W' * H'` with `W', H' ≥ 0` and the same inner dimension agrees with `(W, H)` up to a permutation `σ` and positive scalings `d` of the factors: `W' · a = d a • W · (σ a)` and…

results.title: Nonnegative rank of a matrix
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The nonnegative rank of `X`: the least `r` such that `X = W * H` with `W : m × r` and `H : r × n` entrywise nonnegative (Cohen and Rothblum 1993). If `X` has a negative entry no such factorization exists and the value is the junk value `sInf ∅ = 0`.

results.title: A nonnegative factorization bounds the nonnegative rank
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nonnegative factorization with inner dimension `r` bounds the nonnegative rank by `r`.

results.title: Existence of a factorization of nonnegative-rank inner dimension
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nonnegative matrix has a nonnegative factorization of inner dimension `nonnegRank X`.

results.title: Nonnegative rank is at most the number of columns
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at most its number of columns.

results.title: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at least its rank
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The nonnegative rank of a nonnegative matrix is at least its rank.

results.title: Column sums of a matrix product
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Column sums of a product: `∑ i, (W H) i j = ∑ a, (∑ i, W i a) H a j`.

results.title: Mutational signatures
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Mutational signatures (Alexandrov et al. 2013). Write the mutation-count matrix (mutation types × samples) as `W * H`, signatures (columns of `W`) times exposures `H`. If every signature is a probability vector over mutation types, the total mutation count of sample `j` equals the sum of its exposures.

results.title: Gene-expression deconvolution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write the bulk matrix (genes × samples) as `C * P`, the cell-type profiles `C` times the cell-type proportions `P`. If the proportions of sample `j` are nonnegative and sum to `1` and every cell type expresses gene `g` at a level in `[lo, hi]`, then the bulk level of `g` in sample `j` lies in `[lo, hi]`.
